Milwaukee by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Milwaukee, Wisconsin?

Two city offices split the work. The Assessor's Office, in City Hall Room 507 at 200 E. Wells Street, sets the assessed value of each parcel. The Office of the City Treasurer, in City Hall Room 103, bills and collects the tax. The assessor's number is 414-286-3651 and the treasurer's customer services line is 414-286-2240.

Milwaukee is the county seat of Milwaukee County and sits mostly inside it, although a small part of the city reaches into Waukesha and Washington counties. Because Milwaukee collects its own taxes, a homeowner there pays the city treasurer, not a county office. The bill is a combined one, and a special charge or assessment can be added to it. The treasurer's page warns that unpaid special charges or assessments outstanding in mid-November may be added to the property tax bill, collected as a tax, and cannot be appealed, negotiated or compromised.

The city had an estimated 562,407 residents on July 1, 2025, down 2.7 percent from the April 2020 estimates base, according to the Census Bureau. Only 41.8 percent of housing units are owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024.

When are Milwaukee property taxes due, and how can you pay?

The full amount or the first installment is due by January 31. State law in Wis. Stat. 74.11 sets the default of two equal installments, the first due on or before January 31 and the second on or before July 31, and says a parcel with total tax under $100 is paid in full by January 31. Milwaukee also offers its own longer plan, described below.

The treasurer lists these ways to pay:

  • By mail with a check in the return envelope that comes with the bill. No cash is accepted.
  • At a drop box, such as the one inside City Hall at the Market Street entrance, which is open around the clock.
  • By phone at 414-286-2240 or online, by card with a 2.75 percent convenience fee ($3.00 minimum) or by ACH from a checking or savings account with no fee.
  • Through a bank bill-pay system, sent to City Treasurer, City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street, Milwaukee, WI 53202.

The post office moved its postmarking to regional sorting centers on December 24, 2025, so a letter dropped in a mailbox may not be postmarked that day. The treasurer suggests mailing early, using a drop box, or paying online. Tyler payments made after 4:00 p.m. Central are credited the next business day.

One date to plan around this year: online and telephone payments will be unavailable starting Monday, November 30, 2026 at 4:00 p.m. while the resident access database is updated, and should return after the annual tax bills are created.

Does Milwaukee offer a property tax installment plan?

Yes. The city offers a ten month, interest free installment plan to owners who cannot pay the bill in full. To qualify, the real estate tax bill must be more than $100 and the first installment must be paid by January 31. Owners can sign up for Tyler Auto Pay to have each monthly payment taken from a bank account or card on the due date.

If you sell partway through the ten months, ask the treasurer for the remaining balance and make sure the closing agent has that figure.

What are the key Milwaukee property tax dates?

The table gathers the dates published by the assessor, the treasurer and the state Department of Revenue.

StepDate or periodSource
Assessed values updatedEvery year in mid-AprilCity Assessor
Open Book periodFourth Monday in April to third Monday in MayCity Assessor
Objection form deadlineThird Monday in MayCity Assessor
Tax exemption requestsMarch 1City Assessor
Full payment or first installmentJanuary 31City Treasurer, Wis. Stat. 74.11
Second installment (state default)July 31Wis. Stat. 74.11
Lottery credit claim at the treasurerJanuary 31 after the bill arrivesDepartment of Revenue
Late lottery credit claim to the stateOctober 1 after the bill is issuedDepartment of Revenue

The assessor's page says the deadline to appeal the 2026 assessment has passed. The next Open Book period starts the fourth Monday in April 2027.

How do you appeal a Milwaukee property assessment?

You file a written objection form with the Assessor's Office by the third Monday in May. The preferred route is the Milwaukee Real Property Appeals web application at milwaukee.gov/assessorobjection, which takes new objection forms only during Open Book. You can also mail a paper form to the Assessor's Office, 200 E Wells Street, Room 507, Milwaukee, WI 53202, or drop it off in person Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Emailed forms are not accepted and are treated as not filed.

Evidence can follow the form. The assessor lists these for a house:

  • an appraisal that reflects market conditions as of January 1 of the current year;
  • a market analysis from a local real estate agent for the same date;
  • photos of deferred maintenance as of January 1;
  • photos showing a feature on the property record card was not present on January 1.

An appraiser reviews the appeal and the Board of Assessors makes the determination and mails notice. If you disagree, you may ask the Board of Review clerk for a hearing at boardreview@milwaukee.gov or 414-286-3742. Under Wis. Stat. 70.47, the objector must give the clerk notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the board's first meeting and file the written objection within the first two hours of that meeting, unless the board waives the notice for good cause. Commercial owners who skip the income and expense statement (PR-323) may be barred from testifying before the Board of Review.

What happens if you miss a Milwaukee property tax payment?

The unpaid tax becomes delinquent and interest begins. Under Wis. Stat. 74.47 the interest rate on delinquent general property taxes and special charges is one percent per month or fraction of a month. A county board, or a city authorized under s. 74.87, may also add a penalty of up to 0.5 percent per month by ordinance, so ask the treasurer for the payoff figure.

A first installment not received within five working days after January 31 makes the whole remaining tax delinquent as of February 1 (s. 74.11(7)). The city's interest free plan also depends on the first installment arriving by January 31.

What tax credits and exemptions apply in Milwaukee?

The lottery and gaming credit is the one most homeowners can claim. You must be a Wisconsin resident who owns a dwelling and uses it as a primary residence as of January 1 of the year the taxes are levied. It cannot be claimed on rental units, business property, vacant land or garages, and an owner may claim only one primary residence. For a property inside the city, questions go to the City of Milwaukee treasurer.

If the credit is missing from your bill, apply to the treasurer by January 31 after you receive the bill, or file a late claim with the Department of Revenue by October 1. The credit stays with the property, so the state says its amount should be counted when the tax is prorated between buyer and seller. The assessor also publishes forms for exempt owners, and exemption requests are due March 1.

What should a seller do about the tax bill in Milwaukee?

Find out what is owed before you accept an offer. The treasurer's Resident Access system shows tax bills online, and the assessor's Real Property Search shows the assessed value. The assessor also publishes tax rates for each year from 1984 to the present, so you can see how the rate has moved.

Plan for these points when you sell:

  • Ask the treasurer for the exact balance, including any special charges added in November.
  • Ask your closing agent how the bill is divided between you and the buyer under your contract.
  • Record the deed. The treasurer states that any permanent change in ownership or name must be recorded with the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds.
  • Have the buyer report a mailing address change to the Assessor at City Hall Room 507, or a refund check can go to the previous owner.

The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing of $184,000 for 2020 to 2024 and median gross rent of $1,059. Milwaukee covers 96.18 square miles of land and has 232,520 households. Use these averages only as a starting point.

What is the city of Milwaukee like for homeowners?

Milwaukee lies on the western shore of Lake Michigan at the meeting of the Milwaukee, Menomonee and Kinnickinnic rivers. It was incorporated in 1846 and grew with industry, brewing and manufacturing. Marquette University, the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and the Milwaukee School of Engineering are in the city.

The median household income for 2020 to 2024 was $54,234. About 85.7 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

More questions about Milwaukee, WI Property Tax Guide

When are Milwaukee property taxes due?

The full bill or first installment is due January 31. The state default for a second installment is July 31, and the city also offers a ten month interest free plan if the bill is over $100 and the first installment is paid by January 31.

Where do I pay my Milwaukee property tax bill?

Pay the Office of the City Treasurer at City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street. You can pay by mailed check, a drop box, phone, or online. Cash is not accepted. Online and phone payments go offline on November 30, 2026 at 4:00 p.m.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Milwaukee assessment?

No. The assessor states the 2026 appeal deadline has passed. The deadline is the third Monday in May each year, and Open Book runs from the fourth Monday in April to that date.

What happens if I sell a Milwaukee house with property tax unpaid?

Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff first. Interest on delinquent amounts runs at one percent per month under state law, and the closing agent can pay the balance from your proceeds if your contract allows it.

Does Milwaukee County or the city collect my property tax?

The city does. The City Treasurer collects Milwaukee property tax, and the County Register of Deeds records deeds and collects the state transfer fee.

Challenging your assessment

Objections go to the municipal Board of Review. Confirm the meeting dates with your municipality. Confirm with your county.

The official page we opened lists Page table: City of Waukesha $7.79, Waukesha County $1.30 per $1,000; TOTAL $14.46 and NET RATE $13.42 per $1,000 of valuation (tax year not stated on page; dollar breakdown references 2025).. See the official page.

Local notes

  • Waukesha is in Waukesha County.
Behind on Waukesha property tax?

Get My Cash Offer →

Waukesha by the numbers

Who sends the property tax bill in Waukesha, Wisconsin?

The City of Waukesha Clerk/Treasurer sends the bill and collects the tax, while the City Assessor's Office sets the value the bill is based on. The Clerk/Treasurer department prepares tax bills for property and business owners, collects real estate taxes and keeps the record of Board of Review hearings.

The Assessor's Office discovers, lists and values every taxable property in the city, and it does not levy taxes. A question about the dollar amount on a Waukesha bill goes to the taxing bodies. A question about the value printed on your property record goes to the assessor.

After July 31 the city turns its real estate tax records over to the Waukesha County Treasurer, who collects all delinquent real estate taxes. The county treasurer is at 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Room AC148, Waukesha, WI 53188, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, phone 262-548-7029.

What is the Waukesha property tax rate?

The net rate posted with the 2025 Waukesha tax bills is $13.42 per $1,000 of valuation, which is a gross rate of $14.46 less a state credit of $1.04. Four taxing bodies share the bill, and the city itself keeps a little over half of it.

Taxing jurisdictionLevyRate per $1,000Share of the tax dollar
City of Waukesha$79,645,364$7.7953.8%

Source: City of Waukesha property tax page.

To see what that means for one house, multiply the valuation by the rate. A property valued at $300,000 carries about $4,026 at $13.42 per $1,000. The city says the amounts are set early each December from the levies of the taxing bodies, so the rates for the 2026 bills will appear on the bill that arrives this winter.

When are Waukesha property taxes due?

For the 2025 bills, full payment or the first installment was due January 31, 2026, the second installment March 31, 2026 and the third May 31, 2026. All three of those dates have passed. Waukesha splits the bill into three installments, and the city mails no further bills after the first one, so owners keep the installment coupons that come with it.

The Clerk/Treasurer collects current real estate taxes from mid-December through July 31. The 2026 bills follow the same calendar, which puts them in mailboxes in about a month. When yours arrives, read the due dates printed on it, or call the Clerk/Treasurer at 262-524-3850.

Waukesha's schedule differs from most of its neighbors. The county's due date table shows two dates, January 31 and July 31, for most municipalities in Waukesha County, including the separate Waukesha Village entry. Only the City of Waukesha, New Berlin and Sussex are listed with the three-date plan of January 31, March 31 and May 31. If you own near the city line, check which municipality bills the parcel.

How do you pay a Waukesha property tax bill?

You can pay online, at a Waukesha State Bank branch, by mail, in a drop box or in person at City Hall, and a mortgage lender can pay from escrow. The city lists five ways:

  • Online at tax.waukeshacounty.gov with eCheck ($1.50 fee), debit card ($3.95 fee) or credit card (2.39 percent of the payment).
  • At any Waukesha State Bank branch, with the bill or payment stub. You do not need to be a customer of the bank.
  • By mail to Waukesha City Hall, Attn: Clerk/Treasurer Office, 201 Delafield Street, Waukesha, WI 53188, with the check payable to City of Waukesha.
  • In a 24-hour drop box at City Hall or at the Waukesha Public Library, 321 Wisconsin Avenue. Payments left there are processed the next business day.
  • In person at the Clerk/Treasurer Office on the first floor of City Hall, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

If a mortgage company pays the tax, ask it when the payment will go out. Escrow checks made out to both the city and the homeowner need every named person to sign the back, and a refund of an escrow overage can take four to six weeks by mail.

How does a Waukesha assessment appeal work?

You object to the assessment at the Waukesha Board of Review, and the objection has to be filed before the deadline the city publishes each spring. For 2026 the assessor's office listed this timeline, and every date on it has now passed:

  • Real estate notices issued Friday, May 1, 2026.
  • Open book Monday, May 4, through Friday, May 15, 2026.
  • Board of Review objection deadline Wednesday, May 20, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.
  • First Board of Review hearing Friday, May 22, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

The city described 2026 as a maintenance year. The next assessment date is January 1, 2027, and the assessor's page offers an online Request for Property Review application for that date. State law, which the assessor's page quotes as Wis. Stat. 70.32, directs the assessor to value real property at the full value it could ordinarily bring at a private sale.

The assessor's website also gives a property record card for each parcel, with assessed value, lot size, building details and tax history. Pull it before you list a house, since a buyer's agent will look at the same record.

What happens if a Waukesha property tax bill goes unpaid?

The unpaid balance becomes delinquent and starts to carry interest and penalty. The county treasurer's due date page says an installment plan only works if every installment is paid on time, and a missed one makes the whole remaining balance delinquent under Wis. Stat. 74.11 and 74.12. Delinquent taxes carry interest and penalty of 1.5 percent per month, counted back to February 1 until paid.

A mailed payment counts as timely under Wis. Stat. 74.69(1) if it is properly addressed, postmarked before midnight on the last day to pay and received by the treasurer within five business days after that date. The county notes an exception only for postal delay or administrative error found by a county board committee.

The county treasurer also runs a property tax foreclosure auction on WisconsinSurplus.com. Auction 26-1647 opened November 13, 2026 and closes December 4, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. An owner with a delinquent balance should call 262-548-7029 for the payoff before any sale step goes further.

What should a seller do about Waukesha property tax before closing?

Get the current tax balance from the Clerk/Treasurer or the county treasurer and give it to your closing agent so it appears on the settlement statement. You can see whether a bill is paid at tax.waukeshacounty.gov by entering the address or parcel number.

Two other Wisconsin requirements come up in the same weeks. A seller of a one to four unit home must give the buyer a completed real estate condition report no later than 10 days after the contract is accepted, and the statutory form has a section for taxes, special assessments and permits (Wis. Stat. 709.02 and 709.03). If the report is late, the buyer may rescind within two business days after the 10 days run out. A court-appointed fiduciary who never lived in the house is excused from the report.

For a mortgage payoff, a lender must answer a written request for a payoff statement within seven business days when the loan is on residential property, and it may not describe that payoff amount as subject to change before the payoff date (Wis. Stat. 708.15). Ask for the statement early and match its good-through date to your closing date.

What should a seller know about the city of Waukesha itself?

Waukesha is a city on the Fox River about 15 miles west of Milwaukee, and the city describes itself as the seventh largest in Wisconsin with close to 72,000 residents and the manufacturing hub of Waukesha County. Its total area is 25.07 square miles, about 24.8 of it land.

European-American settlers first arrived in 1834. The area took the name Waukesha on February 8, 1847, the settled center was incorporated as a village in 1852, and the city incorporated in 1896. Its mineral springs made it a well-known Wisconsin watering resort.

The Waukesha School District serves the city with three high schools, Waukesha North, South and West. Carroll University, the oldest college in the state, opened in 1846, and Waukesha County Technical College has a campus downtown. Waukesha Metro Transit runs fixed-route and dial-a-ride service in the city. The 1991 to 2020 climate normals put the January daily mean near 20 degrees Fahrenheit and the July mean near 71.

More questions about Waukesha, WI Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Waukesha property tax?

You pay the City of Waukesha Clerk/Treasurer until July 31, using tax.waukeshacounty.gov, a Waukesha State Bank branch, the mail, a City Hall or library drop box, or the counter at 201 Delafield Street. After July 31 the Waukesha County Treasurer at 515 W. Moreland Blvd. collects what is still owed.

What is the Waukesha property tax rate?

The net rate on the 2025 bills is $13.42 per $1,000 of valuation. That is the $14.46 gross rate of the city, school district, county and technical college, less a $1.04 state credit. The city's own share is $7.79 per $1,000.

Can I pay Waukesha property tax in installments?

Yes. The City of Waukesha offers three installments, which for the 2025 bills fell on January 31, March 31 and May 31, 2026. Missing one makes the remaining balance delinquent, so pay each installment on time or pay in full.

Who hears a Waukesha property assessment appeal?

The Board of Review hears it, and the Clerk/Treasurer keeps its record. The 2026 objection deadline was May 20 and the first hearing was May 22, so both have passed. Watch for the assessment notice that the city issues each spring and file before the stated deadline.

What happens to Waukesha taxes after July 31?

The city sends its unpaid real estate tax records to the Waukesha County Treasurer, who collects the delinquent taxes. Interest and penalty of 1.5 percent per month, counted from February 1, applies to delinquent balances.

title: Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due
content:
Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Wisconsin
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Kenosha Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Kenosha houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Due dates

Kenosha (opened): pay in full by January 31, or by installments Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31. If an installment is late (not received by the City Treasurer within 5 working days) the entire balance becomes delinquent; interest 1% plus 1/2% penalty per month from Feb 1.. See the official page.

Local notes

  • Kenosha is in Kenosha County. Kenosha has a local Board of Assessors step before the Board of Review.
Behind on Kenosha property tax?
We buy Kenosha houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Kenosha by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Kenosha, WI?

The City of Kenosha collects current-year property tax through July 31, and Kenosha County takes over after that. According to the Kenosha County Treasurer's page, every current-year payment made by July 31 is paid to the City of Kenosha, and city parcels paid to the county early are returned. The county takes payments on city parcels for earlier tax years and for balances that are delinquent after July 31.

The county seat is also Kenosha, so the County Treasurer's downtown office at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140 (262-653-2542) is inside the city. That office collects delinquent and prior-year tax on city parcels and runs the tax deed process on parcels that stay unpaid. The treasurer also settles each year with the county's school districts, Gateway Technical College and the Wisconsin Department of Revenue, so a single Kenosha bill carries the levies of several governments.

Most public schools in the city fall under the Kenosha Unified School District, which runs 23 elementary schools, five middle schools, seven charter schools and six high schools according to Wikipedia.

What are the Kenosha property tax due dates?

Kenosha is one of the municipalities that lets owners pay in three installments: January 31, April 30 and July 31. The state rule behind this is Wis. Stat. 74.12, which requires any installment ordinance to collect the first payment by January 31, at least 50 percent of the total by April 30, and everything by July 31. Owners can also pay the full bill in one payment.

InstallmentDate for 2026 taxesWeekend rule
FirstJanuary 31, 2027 (Sunday)Five-working-day window ends Friday, February 5, 2027
SecondApril 30, 2027 (Friday)None needed
ThirdJuly 31, 2027 (Saturday)Window ends Friday, August 6, 2027

Source: Kenosha County Property Tax Payments page for the three dates; Wis. Stat. 74.12(7) and (8) for the weekend rule.

Bills for 2026 should be mailed in December. Under 74.09(5) the mailing deadline is the third Monday of the month, December 21, 2026. Ask the City of Kenosha treasurer to confirm the exact amounts due on each date, since the second and third installments depend on how much you pay earlier.

What happens if a Kenosha installment is late?

The rest of the bill comes due at once and interest begins. A missed first installment makes the whole unpaid tax delinquent on February 1 (74.12(7)). A missed later installment makes the unpaid balance delinquent on the first day of the following month (74.12(8)), with interest and penalty counted from the preceding February 1 under 74.12(10).

Interest is 1 percent a month, and a county can add up to 0.5 percent a month by ordinance (74.47). Kenosha County describes the total as 18 percent a year. Delinquent amounts paid by July 31 go to the city treasurer. After that the city returns its roll to the county treasurer by August 15, and the county collects the balance (74.12(10) and (12)).

The county's guidance for city residents is to call the City of Kenosha treasurer before July 31 and the County Treasurer afterward. If taxes stay unpaid, the county can start a payment plan that requires each delinquent year to be cleared within 10 months. Three years of delinquency opens the tax deed foreclosure process, so a seller with back taxes should resolve them well before that point.

How is a Kenosha property tax bill calculated?

The assessed value, divided by 1,000, is multiplied by the combined mill rate. The WI County Treasurers Association gives the formula this way: total taxes minus the lottery credit and the first dollar credit equal net property taxes, and special assessments and special charges are added to reach the bill. Kenosha County posts current and historical county mill rates on its Property & Taxes page.

Because the rate is per $1,000 of assessed value, each $10,000 added to an assessment adds ten times the mill rate in dollars to the bill. Your bill lists the rate for your parcel and the amount owed to each taxing body, so compare those lines year over year before assuming the city raised its share.

Wisconsin caps how fast a local government's levy can grow. Even so, a bill can jump when your assessment rises, when a special assessment for a street, sewer or sidewalk is added, or when voters approve a referendum. Bills must list recent referendum amounts under 74.09(3)(db).

How do I appeal a Kenosha assessment?

Talk to the City Assessor's Office first, then use the Board of Review if the answer does not change. In cities the board meets in the council chamber or another place the council designates (70.47(1)), within the 45 days that start on the fourth Monday in April. The clerk publishes the meeting notice at least 15 days ahead, or 30 days ahead in a year when the city revalues.

The state's rules for appearing before the board are strict:

  • Give the board clerk written or oral notice of intent at least 48 hours before the first meeting.
  • File the written objection, on the form the board requires, within the first two hours of that meeting.
  • Object to the combined value of land and buildings, since an owner may not contest only one of them.
  • Allow the assessor an exterior view if asked. Under 70.47(7)(aa), an owner who refuses a reasonable certified-mail request loses the right to appear.

After the board rules, a taxpayer has 90 days from receiving the notice of decision to start a certiorari action in court (70.47(13)). The 2026 sessions have ended, so contact the Kenosha assessor early in spring 2027 for the open book dates.

What happens to Kenosha property tax when I sell?

The buyer and seller settle the year's tax through the purchase contract. If the contract is silent, Wis. Stat. 74.15 has the seller reimburse the buyer for the part of the year that passed before closing, measured at one-twelfth of last year's tax per month, with the closing month included if the deed is dated after the 15th. Most Kenosha contracts spell out their own proration, so the title company's figure controls.

A seller who owes tax should ask the city treasurer or, after July 31, the County Treasurer for a payoff good through the closing date. The figure includes interest and penalty, and unpaid special assessments or special charges can pull the whole parcel into delinquency. Mortgage escrow does not change the picture: the county reminds owners that they remain responsible for confirming the lender paid.

State and county programs reduce the bill for some owners. The Lottery and Gaming Credit goes to owners who occupied the home as a primary residence on January 1. The Homestead Credit, filed with state income tax, helps lower-income owners. Disabled veterans can ask the County Veterans Service Office about the state's veterans property tax credit.

What should a seller know about the city of Kenosha itself?

Kenosha sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan, about 32 miles south of Milwaukee and roughly 49 miles north of Chicago. It began as the settlement of Pike Creek in 1835, was renamed Southport, and became the City of Kenosha in 1850. Its 2020 population of 99,986 made it the fourth largest city in Wisconsin, and the Census Bureau estimated 99,239 residents in 2025.

The city grew on the auto industry. Kenosha produced cars and trucks from 1902 to 1988 under names such as Rambler, Nash and American Motors, and the former AMC lakefront plant site is now the HarborPark neighborhood with condominiums, a marina and museums. Snap-on and Jockey International have headquarters in Kenosha, and the University of Wisconsin-Parkside, Carthage College and Gateway Technical College add a student population. Metra commuter rail runs to Chicago, and I-94, WIS 50 and WIS 32 are the main roads. Nearly half the workforce commutes outside Kenosha County.

Locals divide the city into Downtown, Uptown and the area west of I-94. Downtown includes HarborPark and the Allendale neighborhood to the south. Uptown includes Brass, Lincoln Park and Wilson Heights. The climate is humid continental, and blizzards are not unusual: the city recorded about 19 inches of snow in January 1979 and 23.2 inches in the February 2011 blizzard, so buyers often ask about roof and gutter condition.

  • Population estimate, July 1, 2025: 99,239
  • Households, 2020 to 2024: 40,333
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 58.7%
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $225,200
  • Median gross rent: $1,186
  • Median household income: $71,239

Source for the list: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts for Kenosha city, Wisconsin (2020 to 2024 estimates unless noted).

More questions about Kenosha, WI Property Tax Guide

When are Kenosha, WI property taxes due?

Taxes are due in full or in three installments on January 31, April 30 and July 31. The City of Kenosha collects current-year payments through July 31, and the County Treasurer collects after that.

Do I pay Kenosha property tax to the city or the county?

Pay the City of Kenosha for current-year taxes through July 31. Pay the Kenosha County Treasurer for prior-year taxes and for delinquent balances after July 31.

How much interest is charged on late Kenosha property tax?

Interest is 1 percent per month under Wis. Stat. 74.47, and Kenosha County lists the combined interest and penalty as 18 percent a year. The charge starts February 1 for a missed first installment.

Can I sell my Kenosha house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure good through your closing date so the amount can be cleared at closing. Settling delinquent taxes sooner avoids the tax deed process that begins after three years of delinquency.

How do I contest my Kenosha property assessment?

Speak with the City Assessor's Office, then notify the Board of Review clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting and file your objection in the first two hours. Court review by certiorari must begin within 90 days of the board's decision notice.

Who bills what in Racine

  • City of Racine Clerk's Office / Customer Service bills and collects the tax.

  • Racine is in Racine County.

Racine by the numbers

Who bills and who assesses property tax in Racine, Wisconsin?

In Racine, the City Assessor Division sets assessed values, the City collects tax payments through July 31, and the Racine County Treasurer takes over after that. Racine is the county seat of Racine County and sits on Lake Michigan at the mouth of the Root River, 22 miles south of Milwaukee and 60 miles north of Chicago. The 2020 census counted 77,816 residents, the fifth highest of any Wisconsin city.

The Assessor Division is in City Hall, 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. It keeps the city's parcel legal descriptions, ownership, property data, sales data and assessment rolls, and it answers questions on its page at cityofracinewi.gov. Racine County supplies the Ascent Land Records tax search, which owners use to find a parcel's bill.

When are Racine property taxes due?

Racine allows four payments a year: January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31, all paid to the City. The County Treasurer's page confirms that the City collects current-year payments from January 31 through July 31 and that city payment questions go to (262) 636-9171. Bills are mailed in December.

DatePay toSource
January 31City of RacineRacine County Treasurer, property taxes page
March 31City of RacineRacine County Treasurer, property taxes page
May 31City of RacineRacine County Treasurer, property taxes page
July 31City of RacineRacine County Treasurer, property taxes page
After July 31Racine County Treasurer, 730 Wisconsin AveRacine County Treasurer, property taxes page

Most other places in Racine County use only two dates. Racine's four-payment schedule means a seller who closes in spring may have two city payments still open at the closing table.

What if a Racine installment is late or short?

The remaining balance for the year becomes due at once, and the four-payment option is gone. The county says interest and penalties start accruing on February 1 under Wis. Stat. ss. 74.11(7) and 74.12(7), at a combined 1.5 percent per month set by s. 74.47. The county treasurer states that state law gives it no allowance to adjust those amounts.

  • A shortfall of even a small amount on one installment triggers the same result as a missed payment.
  • After July 31 the unpaid balance is payable to the county treasurer, not the City.
  • The county encourages owners with delinquent taxes to arrange regular payments and accepts them.

Before closing a sale, ask both the City and the County which year-by-year amounts remain, since a bill can sit with the city for the current year and with the county for an older one.

How does Racine assess a house?

Wisconsin law requires the city to assess property at market value, and the Assessor Division explains market value as the price a typical, well-informed buyer would pay when neither side is under pressure. The assessor interprets what the market is doing and does not create the value. A revaluation is a full review of every assessment so that values stay uniform.

The division lists the changes that usually raise a value: added rooms or garages, new siding, a substantially modernized kitchen or bath, central air conditioning and extensive remodeling. The law calls for valuing a property from actual view or the best information available. The division says seeing both the inside and outside is best, and when an interior inspection is refused the assessor works from the exterior and from sales of similar properties. Whenever an assessment changes, the law requires the owner to be notified.

How do you appeal a Racine assessment?

Appeal to the Board of Review after the open book period. For 2026 the City held an open book from June 8 to June 12 in Room 308, and the Board of Review met on Tuesday, July 21, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. Both dates have passed, so ask the Assessor Division for the 2027 open book and Board of Review dates.

  • Give notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first board meeting, unless you show good cause during the first two hours of that meeting (s. 70.47(7)(a)).
  • File the written objection in those first two hours, and object to the combined value of land and improvements.
  • Expect to be sworn in. The assessor must be present at the first meeting.
  • Keep in mind the clerk must publish notice at least 15 days beforehand, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

What do you do when an owner sells in Racine?

After a sale, the new owner's name reaches the tax bill through the Assessor's Office, about two weeks after the deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds. The Assessor Division says owner information on bills is normally pulled from the city's database in November, so a house that sells between mid-November and December will still show the old owner on that year's bill. Contact the Assessor's Office for the most current information.

Other forms the division handles include a change of address form, which is available in Room 308 and needs an agent authorization form if someone files for another person. A request to combine or split contiguous parcels you own goes on a separate form. A name change must be recorded with the Register of Deeds, and a recorded survey, if one exists, can be found there too: (262) 636-3208 at 730 Wisconsin Avenue.

Exemption requests must be filed with the Assessor's Office by March 1 to apply to the current assessment year.

What should sellers know about the City of Racine itself?

Racine incorporated as a village on February 13, 1841 and as a city on August 8, 1848. It covers 15.47 square miles of land and uses ZIP codes 53401 to 53408. Industrial names tied to the city include S. C. Johnson and Son, Case IH, Modine Manufacturing, Dremel and InSinkErator, and the Johnson Wax Headquarters by Frank Lloyd Wright is one of its best-known buildings.

The city occupies 15.66 square miles in total at an elevation of 617 feet. The Racine metropolitan area consists solely of Racine County, with about 199,000 residents, and the city has been a factory town almost since its founding.

Which Racine tax relief programs can a homeowner use?

The lottery and gaming credit appears as a reduction on a qualified property tax bill. Owners apply or remove it through the Department of Revenue's online portal, and late-claim forms must be submitted through that portal by October 1. The homestead credit is separate: it is claimed on your Wisconsin income tax return and is aimed at people with lower incomes. Both credits are explained on the Racine County Treasurer's pages, and the county also links a veteran's property tax credit page.

The City of Racine linked the 2026 Wisconsin Department of Revenue Guide for Property Owners from its Assessor page. It covers assessment accuracy, tax procedures and annual valuation updates, which makes it a useful reference if you want the state's own explanation of the process.

How should a Racine owner with unpaid tax prepare to sell?

Collect three numbers first: the current year's unpaid installments owed to the City, any older balance owed to the County Treasurer, and the total interest. Then ask the title company or closing attorney to add them to the payoff statement. An as-is buyer still receives a deed that has to be recorded with the county, so a clear tax balance speeds the closing.

If you inherited the house, tell the Assessor's Office once the deed is recorded so the bill goes to the right name. If the property has several years of delinquent tax, call the County Treasurer and ask about the foreclosure timeline before you list, since the county sells foreclosed properties by sealed bid and over-the-counter sale.

More questions about Racine, WI Property Tax Guide

Who do I pay property tax to in the City of Racine?

Pay the City of Racine on January 31, March 31, May 31 or July 31. After July 31, payments go to the Racine County Treasurer at 730 Wisconsin Avenue. Call the city at (262) 636-9171 with payment questions.

Does Racine allow installments?

Yes. The City of Racine allows four installments, on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Most other places in Racine County allow two.

When does the new owner appear on a Racine tax bill?

The Assessor's Office updates ownership about two weeks after the deed is recorded. Owner names on bills are normally pulled in November, so a sale in mid-November or December may not show on that year's bill.

Where is the Racine Assessor's Office?

It is in City Hall at 730 Washington Avenue, Room 308. The division handles address changes, parcel splits and combines, and exemption requests, which are due March 1.

When is the Racine Board of Review?

The 2026 Board of Review met on July 21, 2026, so that date has passed. Ask the Assessor Division for the 2027 open book and board dates.

Local notes

  • Appleton spans Outagamie (largest), Calumet and Winnebago counties; the city assesses and collects for all parts.

Appleton by the numbers

What should a seller know about Appleton before dealing with property tax?

Appleton is the seat of Outagamie County, on the Fox River about 30 miles southwest of Green Bay and 100 miles north of Milwaukee. The 2020 census counted 75,644 residents in 24.82 square miles, which makes it the sixth most populous city in Wisconsin. The city was settled in 1847 and incorporated in 1857, and papermaking shaped its economy after the first mill opened in 1853. Today the largest employers include St. Elizabeth Hospital, Thrivent Financial and the Appleton Area School District, which runs Appleton East, North and West high schools.

Two facts about the map matter for a tax bill. First, Appleton is not entirely inside one county: most of it lies in Outagamie County, with smaller pieces in Calumet and Winnebago counties. Second, the city sits in five school districts, so the assessor keeps more than one tax rate and assessment level. Winters are long: the NOAA normals show about 49 inches of snow a year and a record low of minus 32 degrees.

Who assesses and who bills property tax in Appleton?

The city does both, through two offices, and the county gets involved only when a bill goes delinquent.

  • Assessor's Office, (920) 832-5850. Values every parcel, keeps ownership and lot descriptions, and mails notices when an assessment changes. The office revalues all property at least once every five years and tries to inspect each property at least once every ten.
  • Finance Department, (920) 832-6442. Bills and collects the tax at City Hall, 100 N. Appleton St. Bills can be paid at the first-floor desk or drive-up window on weekdays, in the night deposit box, by mail to P.O. Box 2519, Appleton, WI 54912-2519, or online through the Payment Center. The online processor charges a convenience fee that the city does not receive.
  • City Clerk, (920) 832-6443. Takes notices of intent to object and objection forms for the Board of Review.

The city Finance page also links to the real estate tax page where a copy of your bill and a breakdown of where the money goes are posted. Your tax is the net tax rate per $1,000 multiplied by your assessed value, and the rate is set by the combined budgets of the school district, city, county, sewer district, technical college and state reforestation.

When are Appleton property tax bills due?

Appleton lets owners pay in four installments due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31, with the dates printed on the bill. State law sends bills out by the third Monday in December. A late payment on any installment cancels the installment option and adds monthly interest calculated from February 1 on the unpaid balance, as required by state law. Under Wis. Stat. 74.47 that interest is one percent per month, and a county board can add a penalty of up to half a percent per month.

Once a balance is delinquent, the city no longer collects it. The city says unpaid balances from 2025 and earlier years go to the county treasurer for the county where the parcel sits.

Part of Appleton2020 residentsCounty treasurer for delinquent tax
Outagamie County62,899(920) 832-5065
Calumet County11,304(920) 849-1457
Winnebago County1,441(920) 232-3420

Sources: City of Appleton Finance Department for the phone numbers; 2020 census counts as reported for Appleton.

If you pay in person with an escrow check and are owed a refund of $750 or less, you may receive it in cash. Larger refunds, and any refund on a mailed or drop-box payment, are mailed within four to six weeks. Escrow checks made out to the owner and the City of Appleton must be endorsed by both.

How does the Appleton assessment and appeal process work?

The city mails a Notice of Changed Assessment in spring, then runs an informal review before the formal Board of Review. In 2026 the notices went out April 9, Open Book ran April 13 to April 22, and the Board of Review met April 29 in Council Chambers on the sixth floor of City Hall, after which the 2026 assessments became final. Ask the Assessor for the 2027 calendar once it is posted. By law a notice must go out at least 15 days before the board meets, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

To object, follow the steps the Clerk lists:

  • Talk to the Assessor first. The Clerk lists this as step one.
  • Give the City Clerk written or oral notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting.
  • File Objection Form PA-115A within the first two hours of that first meeting.
  • Bring evidence. The Board starts from the assumption that the assessor's value is correct, and the burden is on the owner.

The Wisconsin Department of Revenue explains the same rules on its board of review page. The board has seven members: the Mayor, the City Clerk, three alderpersons and three residents. A decision can be taken to circuit court by certiorari within 90 days of the notice of decision under Wis. Stat. 70.47.

The Assessor's office warns that by the time the December tax bill arrives it is too late to object, and that paying under protest does not count as an objection unless you first appealed to the Board of Review.

Which credits reduce an Appleton tax bill?

Two state credits appear on the bill. The lottery and gaming credit goes to an owner who used the home as a primary residence on January 1 of the year taxes are levied, and the amount changes yearly. The first dollar credit applies automatically to every taxable parcel with an improvement on it, whether or not the owner lives there. Ask the county treasurer for your county about the lottery credit.

The assessment itself also responds to what you do to the house. Appleton's Assessor says routine work such as a new furnace, roof repair, gutters or patching walls generally does not raise the assessment, although several such items together might. Additions, finished basements, new decks and extensive kitchen or bath remodels usually do. Assessors also walk through recently sold homes each fall and winter, so expect a letter after a sale.

What fees apply when I sell an Appleton house?

Wisconsin charges the seller a real estate transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value, set by Wis. Stat. 77.22. On a $250,000 sale that is $750. The Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded, and an electronic transfer return signed by buyer and seller must be filed first. Outagamie County, Calumet County or Winnebago County handles the recording depending on where the parcel sits.

Some conveyances are exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25, and the reason must be written on the face of the deed. Examples include transfers by will, descent or survivorship, transfers under a foreclosure or a deed in lieu to the mortgage holder, sales for delinquent taxes, and transfers between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild for nominal or no consideration. A normal sale to a buyer is not on the list.

How do I clear unpaid Appleton property tax before a sale?

Ask the title or escrow company to order a payoff from the correct treasurer. For the current bill that is the Finance Department. For 2025 and earlier years it is the county treasurer, and the payoff includes interest charged from February 1. Under Wisconsin's delinquent tax statutes, delinquent real property tax can be discharged by paying the delinquent amount with interest and any penalty before a tax certificate is issued on the parcel.

Do not wait for the bill if a sale will close near a deadline. Tell your closing agent which installments are paid. If the house has been in the family for years and the tax history is unclear, a call to the Finance Department with the parcel number is the fastest way to see what is open.

More questions about Appleton, WI Property Tax Guide

When are Appleton property taxes due?

In four installments on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Missing an installment cancels the installment option and starts interest from February 1. Pay at City Hall, by mail, in a drop box or online.

Which county treasurer do I pay if my Appleton taxes are delinquent?

The county where the parcel sits: Outagamie at (920) 832-5065, Calumet at (920) 849-1457 or Winnebago at (920) 232-3420. The city sends unpaid balances for 2025 and earlier years to that treasurer.

How do I appeal my Appleton assessment?

Talk to the Assessor at (920) 832-5850, then give the City Clerk notice of intent at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting and file Objection Form PA-115A in the first two hours of that meeting. The 2026 meeting was April 29, so 2027 dates will be set by the city.

Who pays the Wisconsin transfer fee when an Appleton home sells?

The seller. The fee is 30 cents per $100 of value and is collected by the Register of Deeds at recording. Transfers by inheritance, foreclosure deeds and some family conveyances are exempt.

Can I pay property tax under protest instead of appealing?

No. The Assessor states that paying under protest is not an objection unless you first filed an appeal with the Board of Review. The objection has to happen in spring, before the December bill arrives.
